extracted.intended_audience: aspiring literary/art critics, aesthetes, and writers interested in theory of criticism and artistic practice
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive and philosophical principles about what makes a critic and what constitutes good art — covering temperament, the primacy of form, the critic's role, and the relationship between art, ethics, and society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness is not a quality of the true critic
rubrics_metrics.description: A critic cannot be fair in the ordinary sense of the word; an unbiassed opinion is usually valueless and having preferences is appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critic must surrender absolutely to the work and be dominated by it for the time; fairness (in the sense of impartial admiration for all schools) is more suited to an auctioneer than a true critic. The passage stresses that impartiality is neither necessary nor desirable for genuine criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticism is not (primarily) a rational activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Reason is not the faculty to which Art appeals; Art creates a kind of 'divine madness' and must be loved beyond reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are two ways of disliking art: simple dislike or liking it 'rationally.' Since art appeals to emotion and inspires rather than springs from reason, rational assessment alone is insufficient for criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity must be tempered in criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: A little sincerity is dangerous; a great deal is fatal. The critic should be sincere in devotion to beauty but avoid rigid, single-minded sincerity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The true critic seeks beauty in every age and school, avoids being limited by settled customs or stereotyped modes of looking at things, and multiplies personalities through change rather than remaining a slave to fixed opinions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep Art and Ethics strictly separate
rubrics_metrics.description: The spheres of Art and Ethics are distinct and separate; conflating them brings chaos and corrupts aesthetic judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethical or moral indignation should not determine artistic value. Modern Puritans and prurient journalism may temporarily taint beauty, but moral considerations cannot set limits to the artist. Critics must recognise the autonomy of aesthetic judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperament is the primary requisite for the critic
rubrics_metrics.description: An exquisite temperament susceptible to beauty — a separate beauty-sense apart from reason and soul — is the first and most important qualification of a critic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This sense may lead some to create and others to contemplate; it requires cultivation and an environment of fair sights and sounds (Plato's pedagogy) to develop into a reliable critical instinct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate taste via environment and education
rubrics_metrics.description: Exquisite environment and early exposure to beauty are necessary to form and perfect the aesthetic sense and critical spirit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato's prescription for education (surrounding youth with fair sights and sounds) is cited; particulars such as loitering in cloisters or meditative contact with harmonious architecture and nature are given as examples of environments that cultivate taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decorative arts are central to cultivating temperament
rubrics_metrics.description: For the cultivation of temperament one should turn to the decorative arts — arts that 'touch' us and are suitable for daily life rather than those that merely teach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decorative art creates mood and temperament, develops the sense of form which underlies both creative and critical accomplishment, and prepares the soul for imaginative work. It is contrasted with some modern pictures which are 'too clever' or impossible to live with.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer form-to-content: form precedes feeling and idea
rubrics_metrics.description: The real artist proceeds from form to thought and passion (not from feeling to form); form suggests what is to fill it and makes work complete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: sonnet-scheme suggesting modes of music and rhyme; the claim that finding expression intensifies emotion and that Form creates passion and even mitigates pain. The passage argues for formal discipline as the source of artistic inspiration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pure 'natural' feeling; sincerity of feeling often spoils art
rubrics_metrics.description: All bad poetry springs from genuine feeling; being natural is obvious and inartistic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'real passion' would ruin certain artists; actual events often spoil art. The aesthetic values crafted form over raw emotion to prevent obviousness and sentimentality.

rubrics_metrics.name: The artist is a poor judge of other arts (and often of his own)
rubrics_metrics.description: A truly great artist can never properly judge other people's work and can hardly judge his own, because creative concentration limits appreciative faculty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creation narrows vision while contemplation widens it. Historical examples: Wordsworth and Shelley misunderstood each other; Milton couldn't understand Shakespeare's method; painters and poets often fail to appreciate different modes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art appeals to the universal artistic temperament, not the specialist
rubrics_metrics.description: Art's claim is universality; it does not primarily address the specialist artist but the broader artistic temperament which may span forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus the aesthetic critic, not the practicing artist, is in the position to appreciate diverse forms and modes of art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technique is personality and cannot be taught like a craft
rubrics_metrics.description: Each art has its grammar and materials, but Technique is really personality: the pupil cannot be taught it by the artist, though the aesthetic critic can understand it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While laws of art are fixed, their true realization requires imaginative touch; this is why artists cannot systematically teach their unique technique, and why critics — who apprehend forms — are able to analyze technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticism is a creative, necessary, and expanding art
rubrics_metrics.description: The subject-matter available to creation is diminishing while that of criticism increases; Criticism 'imposes form upon chaos' and is needed more as the world advances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because familiar backgrounds have been exhausted, creation must become more critical; criticism supplies new attitudes and points of view and thus has a vital and growing role in cultural life.

rubrics_metrics.name: A critic's influence comes from embodying an ideal age's culture
rubrics_metrics.description: The critic's influence is primarily the fact of his own existence as the flawless type; he should aim to perfect himself and awaken the age rather than reform individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: His concern should be with the age — creating larger vision and nobler moods — rather than attempting to reform particular celebrated or established individuals, whose reformation would be painful and unlikely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticism distils culture and makes historical understanding possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism concentrates creative work into an essence usable for culture; where records are absent, criticism can re-create the past from small fragments (philological/archaeological criticism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism guides readers through the mass of books and art, and can, like science reconstructing extinct creatures, reconstruct mental life and cultural origins from small remains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticism fosters cosmopolitanism by revealing unity of mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Intellectual criticism, insisting on the unity of the human mind in variety of its forms, will help annihilate race-prejudices and bind nations together culturally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Goethe's example: he remained culturally appreciative of other nations despite national loyalties. The passage suggests cultural appreciation (e.g., for French prose) will undercut hatred and lead to peace founded on understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticism creates a philosophic temper that loves truth for itself
rubrics_metrics.description: By refusing to adopt final positions or bind itself to sectarian shibboleths, Criticism creates a serene philosophic temper that loves truth though it knows it to be unattainable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This temper is contrasted with English fanaticism and rage; scientific temper exemplified (Darwin) as calm, reasoned thinking rather than fanatic sincerity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetics are higher than ethics; assessment of art is not moral judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Æsthetics belong to a more spiritual sphere than Ethics; a sense of beauty is a higher development for the individual than mere notions of right and wrong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy with sexual vs natural selection: ethics make existence possible, aesthetics make life lovely and provide progress, variety and change. Thus art should not be judged primarily by ethical standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalism and popular moralists should not regulate artistic subject-matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspapers and moralistic commentators (Tartuffes) who chronicle sordid facts or moralize should not be allowed to set limits on what artists may present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While journalism has value (keeping us in touch with ignorance, chronicling events), it becomes stultifying when it allows uninformed moralists to write about modern art; such interference risks reducing art to the prosaic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Costume, stage design and decorative detail are integral to theatrical illusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Shakespeare relies heavily on costume and elaborate stage directions for illusion; dress and masques are introduced for the pleasure they give the eye and for illusionist effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that 'the play and the play only' matters are mistaken; historical evidence in Shakespeare's stage-directions and the inclusion of masques and dances shows that visual elements are central to producing theatrical illusion.
